method: The fragment was written with no web search; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, strongest claims first: the founding years, the people and their dates, the classification, the sites, the grapes, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

Every source address the draft listed was tested; where a search never returned it, it was replaced by a page a search did return, so every source in the fragment is one the refuter saw. All sources are read: search (a result summary, from the body's own domain where marked primary).
A fact found in two independent sources or one primary stands; a fact found in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches.

changed.was: Joseph Krug (1800 to 1866), born in Mainz, learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own in Reims in 1843. In 1848 he set down his creed in a personal notebook: to make, every year and whatever the weather, the fullest expression of Champagne by blending the wines of many plots and many years. For more than a century that blend was sold as Private Cuvée, and in 1978 the house renamed it Grande Cuvée. The family added a vintage, a rosé and, from the walled Clos du Mesnil, a Chardonnay of one vineyard first made from the 1979 vintage, but the blend remained the house's purpose. Krug kept fermenting in small oak casks while most houses turned to steel tanks, and it built a library of reserve wines from many years for the cellar master to draw on. In 2016 the house began to give each release an Édition number, so that a guest can tell one year's Grande Cuvée from the next and read the harvest it was built around. A sommelier sells it as a wine to be tasted, not a toast to be drunk.
changed.now: Joseph Krug (1800 to 1866), born in Mainz, learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own in Reims in 1843. In 1848, as the house tells it, he set down his creed in a personal notebook: to make the fullest expression of Champagne every year, whatever the weather, by blending the wines of many plots and many years. His son took over at his death in 1866, the year the house moved to the Rue Coquebert in Reims. Until 1978 the blend was sold as Private Cuvée; that year the house renamed it Grande Cuvée. Beside it the house made vintage wines, and in the 1970s it added a rosé and, from the walled Clos du Mesnil bought in 1971, a Chardonnay of one vineyard first made from the 1979 vintage, but the blend remained the house's purpose. Krug kept fermenting in small oak casks while most houses turned to steel tanks, and it built a library of reserve wines from many years for the cellar master to draw on. In the 2010s the house began to print an Édition number on the front label, so that a guest can tell one year's Grande Cuvée from the next and read the harvest it was built around. A sommelier sells it as a wine to be tasted, not a toast to be drunk.
changed.why: Private Cuvée until 1978 (two sources) in place of more than a century (one); the son and the Rue Coquebert in 1866; vintage wines made before the rosé of the 1970s; Clos du Mesnil bought in 1971 (the house); the Édition on the front label in the 2010s, from the 163rd, not 2016.

changed.was: Claude Moët (1683 to 1760) founded his wine house at Épernay in 1743, and his grandson Jean-Rémy Moët (1758 to 1841) carried its wines across Europe and counted the Emperor Napoleon among his customers. In 1833 a son-in-law of the Chandon family became a partner and the house took the name Moët & Chandon. Its prestige cuvée honours Dom Pierre Pérignon (1638 to 1715), cellarer of the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death. He did not invent sparkling Champagne: he blended grapes from different villages, refined the pressing of black grapes for white juice and, like the winemakers of his day, tried to keep bubbles out of the wine. The name Dom Pérignon belonged to the house of Mercier, which passed it to Moët after a marriage between the two families in 1927. The first Dom Pérignon, from the 1921 vintage, was released in 1936. It has since been made only in declared years, and the house releases the same vintage a second and a third time, as Plénitudes, after far longer ageing on the lees.
changed.now: An Épernay wine merchant of the Moët family founded the house in 1743, and his grandson Jean-Rémy Moët (1758 to 1841) carried its wines across Europe; the Emperor Napoleon (1769 to 1821) visited him at Épernay and awarded him the Légion d'honneur. In 1833 the house passed to Jean-Rémy's son and his son-in-law, a Chandon, and took the name Moët & Chandon. Its prestige cuvée honours Dom Pierre Pérignon, cellarer of the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death in 1715. He did not invent sparkling Champagne, a tale first told in 1821, long after his death: he blended grapes from different vineyards and, by most accounts, refined the making of white wine from black grapes, while the wines his abbey sold did not sparkle. The name Dom Pérignon belonged to the house of Mercier, which passed it to Moët after a marriage between the two families in 1927. The first Dom Pérignon, from the 1921 vintage, was released in 1936. It has since been made only in declared years, and the house releases the same vintage a second and a third time, as Plénitudes, after far longer ageing on the lees.
changed.why: Claude Moët's dates unfound; Napoleon a visitor and giver of the Légion d'honneur, not a customer; 1833 to the son and son-in-law; the monk dated by 1668 and 1715; the bubbles tale of 1821 and the abbey's still wines in place of trying to keep bubbles out; the pressing of black grapes hedged.

changed.was: The house that became Louis Roederer was a Reims wine business recorded in 1776. A nephew of its owner inherited it in 1833 and gave it his own name, Louis Roederer, and under him and his son the house sold widely in Russia. In 1876 Tsar Alexander II (1818 to 1881) asked the house to set aside its prestige cuvée for his court each year, and it was bottled in clear glass with a flat base so that, as the story is told, nothing could be hidden in the bottle or its punt. The wine took its name, Cristal, from that glass. The revolution of 1917 took from the house its first customer and much of its Russian trade, and Cristal later became a wine any guest could order; a rosé followed in 1974. Unlike most houses, Roederer built its prestige wine on its own vineyards rather than on bought grapes, and Cristal is still made only in the years the house judges ripe enough. The coloured cellophane round each bottle is there to keep light from a wine in clear glass.

changed.was: Bollinger was founded at Aÿ in 1829 by three partners, one of them a young German salesman whose name the house carries. It received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria in 1884, and British drinkers have followed it ever since. After her husband's death in 1941, Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), ran the house through the German occupation and on until 1971. She cycled through the vineyards to inspect them, bought more vines and launched R.D., a vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old barrels, holding its reserve wines in magnum under cork and tending two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir inside Aÿ, the source of Vieilles Vignes Françaises. La Grande Année is the wine in which all of that shows: a vintage of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, fermented in barrel, aged under cork and riddled by hand, from a house that has stayed in the founding family's line.
changed.now: Bollinger was founded at Aÿ in 1829 by three partners, one of them a young German from Württemberg whose name the house carries. It received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria (1819 to 1901) in 1884. After her husband's death in 1941, Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), ran the house through the German occupation and on until 1971. She cycled through the vineyards to inspect them, released R.D. in 1967, a 1952 vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees, and in 1969 made the first Vieilles Vignes Françaises. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old barrels, holding part of its reserve wines in magnum under cork and tending two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir inside Aÿ, the source of Vieilles Vignes Françaises. La Grande Année is the wine in which all of that shows: a vintage of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, fermented in barrel, aged under cork for years and riddled by hand, and made only in the years the house declares.
changed.why: Württemberg, not a salesman; Queen Victoria dated; the British following and the bought vines cut; R.D. 1967 and Vieilles Vignes Françaises 1969 dated; part of the reserve in magnum; no closing claim on ownership.

changed.was: Jacques Selosse is a small domaine in Avize, in the Côte des Blancs, whose family began bottling its own Champagne around 1960, by most accounts, rather than selling all its grapes to the houses. In 1980 the founder's son took charge. He had trained in Burgundy and brought its ways back to Champagne: low yields, ploughed soils, wild yeasts, fermentation in barrels and a wine made first as a wine of place and only then as a sparkling wine. In the mid 1980s, inspired by time spent in Jerez, he began a solera of Avize Chardonnay, in 1986 by most accounts: each year the new wine goes into the reserve and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so the blend carries a little of every year since it began. That wine is Substance. Its oxidative, nutty depth divided drinkers, but it made Selosse the model for the grower movement of the 1990s and 2000s, when small estates across Champagne began to bottle their own wines and to name their villages and plots on the label.
changed.now: Jacques Selosse is a small domaine in Avize, in the Côte des Blancs, set up by its founder after the Second World War, in 1949 by several accounts. The family first made and bottled Champagne of its own in the years around 1960, rather than selling all its grapes to the houses. The founder's son, who had studied at the wine school in Beaune, joined him in 1974 and took charge in 1980. He brought Burgundy's ways back to Champagne: low yields, native yeasts, fermentation in barrels and a wine made first as a wine of place and only then as a sparkling wine. In 1986, by most accounts, he began a perpetual reserve of Avize Chardonnay on the model of a Sherry solera: each year the new wine goes into the reserve and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so the blend carries a little of every year since it began. That wine is Substance. Its oxidative, nutty depth divided drinkers, but it made Selosse the model for the grower movement of the 1990s and 2000s, when small estates across Champagne began to bottle their own wines and to name their villages and plots on the label.
changed.why: The founding hedged (1949 in several accounts); the son joined in 1974 and took charge in 1980; Beaune; ploughed soils and Jerez cut; the solera on the Sherry model.
